creative.body:
I've now spent more on enema kits than I have on my actual Mounjaro prescription. And they stop working after the third one.

I need to say that out loud because I haven't said it to anyone. Not my husband. Not my doctor. Not even the women in my GLP-1 Facebook group who share everything.

Because when you're buying Fleet saline enemas in bulk from Amazon so the cashier at CVS doesn't see your face again, you've crossed a line you didn't know existed. And once you cross it, you just... stop talking about it.

Let me back up.

I started Mounjaro in June. By August I'd lost twenty-two pounds and my coworkers were asking what I was doing different. By September I hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days and I was lying on the bathroom tile at midnight wondering if I should wake my husband or call 911.

I didn't do either. I drove to a 24-hour Walgreens in my pajamas and bought my first enema kit at 12:40 AM.

It worked. Painfully. Violently. But it worked. And I remember thinking, as I sat on the bathroom floor afterward, sweating and shaking and crying a little — okay. That's handled. Back to normal.

It wasn't back to normal.

Within two weeks, I needed another one. Two weeks after that, another. Then the gap closed to ten days. Then eight. Then I started keeping one in my overnight bag when we visited my in-laws because I couldn't risk being away from home without a backup plan.

I want you to understand what that feels like. Packing an enema kit next to your toothbrush. Wondering if your mother-in-law will find it in the bathroom trash. Planning your entire week around whether or not your body will cooperate.

I was losing weight. People kept telling me how great I looked. And I was giving myself enemas on a schedule like it was a medical treatment I'd prescribed myself.

Around month four, the enemas started taking longer to work. The first time I used one and nothing happened for forty-five minutes, I panicked. I used a second one the same night. That's when I Googled "enema dependency GLP-1" and realized I wasn't the only one. Not even close.

There are entire threads. Hundreds of women describing the exact same escalation. Miralax didn't work. Moved to enemas. Enemas worked until they didn't. Now what?

That "now what" sat in my chest for weeks.

I was scrolling one of those threads at 2 AM — because that's when you do your most honest research, when nobody's watching — and a comment stopped me cold. It was from a retired gastroenterologist. Verified in the group. He'd been answering questions for months, no product to sell, no agenda. Just explaining things in plain language that no one's doctor had apparently bothered to explain.

He wrote one line that rewired my entire understanding of what was happening inside me.

"You're all treating the bottom. The problem is at the top."

I stared at that sentence for a long time.

Then he explained it. Your GLP-1 works by slowing your stomach down. That's how it controls appetite. But when the stomach slows down too much, food doesn't move into the intestines on schedule. Everything downstream backs up. Not because your colon stopped working. Because your stomach stopped sending food through.

Laxatives pull water into the colon. That's the bottom. Fiber adds bulk to the colon. That's the bottom. Enemas flush the colon. That's the bottom.

Every single thing I'd tried — every single thing any of us had tried — was working six feet downstream from where the problem actually started.

It was like finding out you've been mopping the floor under a leak for four months instead of fixing the pipe.

I screenshotted that comment and couldn't sleep. Not because I was upset. Because for the first time, the pattern made sense. The Miralax failing. The fiber making bloating worse. The enemas needing to be stronger and more frequent. All of it. Every failed attempt was aimed at the wrong place.

So I started reading. Not Reddit threads at 2 AM anymore — actual research. What helps the stomach move food through when it's been slowed down by medication?

Three things kept showing up.

The first was motility support. Something that helps wake the stomach back up and keep food moving into the intestines instead of sitting there. Not a stimulant laxative. Not something that forces contractions in the colon. Something that works where the slowdown actually happens.

The second was digestive enzyme support. When food sits in a slowed stomach for too long, it ferments. That's where the bloating comes from, the gas, the pressure. Enzymes help break food down faster so even in a slower system, food gets processed instead of rotting.

The third was something to soothe the gut lining. Months of backup, inflammation, and repeated laxative use had left everything irritated. The lining needed to calm down before anything else could work properly.

I spent two weeks looking for a product that combined all three. I already knew what I didn't want — another pile of capsules on my nightstand. I was taking six different supplements at one point. Magnesium citrate, a probiotic I picked at random, Miralax every other day, Gas-X, and two different fiber powders. None of them aimed at the stomach. All of them aimed at the colon.

Most products I found had one of the three things. A motility supplement here. A digestive enzyme there. Nothing that addressed all three in the same place.

Then I found Motilli.

Celery juice gummies designed specifically for people on GLP-1s. I almost scrolled past it because I'd been burned by "gut health" gummies before. But I checked the formula against my checklist. Motility support. Digestive enzyme support. Gut lining support. All three. In a gummy I could actually stomach on days when swallowing a capsule made me gag.

I ordered it expecting nothing. I'd been managing my own body with saline enemas for four months. A gummy felt almost insulting.

The first week, nothing changed. I wrote it off.

Day ten, I had a bowel movement without any intervention. No Miralax. No enema. No lying on the bathroom floor bargaining with my own intestines. Just... went. Like a normal person. I almost didn't trust it.

Day sixteen, it happened again. Then day nineteen. Then it started becoming something I didn't have to think about at all.

By the end of the second month, I threw away the Fleet boxes under the sink. All of them. I didn't even do it ceremonially. I just tossed them in the trash on a Tuesday while I was cleaning the bathroom. It felt like nothing. It was everything.

My husband doesn't know any of this. He doesn't know about the 2 AM Walgreens trips. He doesn't know about the enema kits in my overnight bag. He doesn't know that I used to calculate how many days it had been since I'd gone to the bathroom and then plan our entire weekend around whether I'd need to "deal with it" before we went anywhere.

He just knows I seem happier. Less anxious. That I said yes to the lake house trip without hesitating for the first time in six months.

Last weekend I ate a full meal before my son's baseball game and didn't think about it once. Didn't calculate. Didn't pack anything in my purse. Didn't plan an escape route to the nearest bathroom. Just ate and went and watched my kid play.

That's what it's supposed to feel like.

I'm not telling you the enemas were wrong. When you're in crisis, you do what you have to do. I'm telling you they were aimed at the wrong end. And as long as you keep treating the bottom, you're going to keep escalating. Miralax to enemas. Enemas once a month to enemas once a week. And eventually, the enemas stop working too. Then you're sitting in another 2 AM Google search wondering what's left.

There's something left. And it's not at the bottom.

You can keep treating the bottom. Keep escalating. Keep hiding kits under the sink and planning your week around whether your body will cooperate.

Or you can fix the part that's actually broken.

I don't hide anything under the sink anymore.
creative.title: I Packed an Enema Kit Next to My Toothbrush for 4 Months Before I Learned Where GLP-1 Constipation Actually Starts.
